title: The kea

paragraphs.text: The calls of the kea echo throughout the rock canyons and exposed cliffs which are its favoured haunts, often well above the treeline in the snow-covered country of the South Island of New Zealand. No other parrot worldwide makes its home in the mountains. Keas range over about four million hectares throughout the mountains of the South Island, and can be found from coastal dunes to high alpine peaks. They are absent from both the North Island and Stewart Island of New Zealand. Keas mainly nest within native forests, and it is thought that they may play an important role in dispersing seeds of alpine plants. They forage for food in all types of native forest, sub-alpine scrub and grassy hills. They socialise on prominently exposed rocks, and are frequently reported in pine forests adjacent to native forests.

The kea is a large, olive-green-coloured parrot with scarlet underwings and a slender grey-black bill, suitable for probing the ground to extract roots, bulbs and shoots. The female body mass is about 20% less than that of the male kea and the female's bill is shorter. Juveniles have yellow eyelids, which fade to grey as the bird matures. The kea's call is a long, loud, high-pitched descending cry which may be broken 'kee-ee-aa-aa', or unbroken 'keeeeeaaaa'. Many quiet contact calls are given. Juvenile calls are less stable in tone, being more of a loud uncontrolled whooping.

Keas are monogamous, with long-term pairs nesting mainly below the treeline, on the ground in natural cavities such as a rock crevice, the hollow base of a large tree, a hollow under the roots of a tree or a dirt cavity under the edge of an old river terrace.Usually four eggs are laid between July and January (peak laying in August-October).Incubation takes 22-24 days, and chicks stay in the nest for three months. The female does all the incubation, brooding and feeding of the young by regurgitation. The male brings food to the female, feeding her near the nest site. Normally eggs are laid once a year. An individual female may nest in several successive years, but not all females nest every year. Juveniles are tolerated by unrelated adults and this facilitates the chick's learning of complex skills which they will later use for foraging. Juveniles 'play', and the juvenile period is long compared to that of other parrots.

Adaptability is a key part of kea ecology. Distinctive traits of keas compared to other parrots include the slender bill, ground nesting, winter breeding, social dynamics, intelligence, prolonged juvenile phase and use of alpine habitat. This combination of traits indicates an evolutionary history in an unforested habitat.

Estimating kea population size is difficult due to their extensive range, the rocky and uneven landscape, the cryptic behaviour of adults and the flocking behaviour of the young. Density in the upland forest of Nelson Lakes National Park was recently estimated as approximately one adult female kea per 2,750 hectares, down from about one per 550 hectares a decade earlier. Arthur's Pass National Park holds possibly ten times the density of Nelson Lakes. In a forest in the Westland region the density is roughly one adult female per 500 hectares. A conservative estimate of one adult female per 2,000 hectares of forest gives a total population of 4,000 adults (males plus females). Productivity estimates predict about one juvenile for every breeding pair, giving a total population of about 6,000 birds, a figure that would seem accurate. Other commonly cited estimates are 15,000 and 1,000 to 5,000. Both of these seem extreme given recent survey data.

The kea gained early notoriety among settler farmers for attacks on their sheep. Their attraction to people and their belongings is a two-edged sword, providing both new threats and new opportunities. Keas' instinctive curiosity attracts them to humans wherever people enter the parrot’s domain. Consequently, the birds are a feature at South Island ski fields and man-made huts. They have benefited from some human-induced modifications to their habitat, including scavenging from tourists and hunters, and turning over soil in search of grubs to feed on in both pine forestry areas and land that is cultivated.

Hunting of keas as a measure to protect sheep was outlawed in 1971, and full protection was finally granted in 1986.Contemporary threats include introduced mammalian predators, environmental lead, and conflict and accidents with humans and their equipment. Keas are also killed accidentally in possum traps and by poison baits deployed to control predators. The conservation status of this species was changed from naturally uncommon to nationally endangered in 2013.Unfortunately, the very nature of the kea, which has enabled the species to adapt to its extreme environment, means it is quite fearless and this unfortunately may increase its chance of being trapped or poisoned.
